## The problem

Our team of twelve now maintains feature branches that routinely live for two to three weeks before merging. By the time a branch reaches review, it has drifted so far from main that merges regularly break unrelated work, and reviewers are asked to evaluate sprawling diffs they can't reasonably reason about in one sitting. Integration has become something we fear rather than something we do continuously, and that fear pushes teams toward even longer branches, which makes the next integration worse. We are spending review cycles reconciling merge conflicts instead of discussing design, and bugs caused by divergent assumptions across branches are surfacing in production days after the code was actually written.

## The proposal

I'm proposing we move to trunk-based development: everyone commits small, reviewed changes directly to main at least once a day, protected by feature flags for anything incomplete. Concretely:

- All new work lands on main within 24 hours of starting, gated by flags when unfinished
- CI must stay green on main at all times, with a fast rollback path for any regression
- PRs are capped at roughly 400 lines to keep review meaningful and fast
- We invest in a feature-flag system before rollout, not after
- We run a two-week pilot with one squad before asking the full team to switch

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: trunk-based development demands stronger test coverage and CI discipline than we currently have, and without that safety net, frequent small merges to main could destabilize it faster than long branches ever did. Some engineers will also worry that half-finished features behind flags accumulate as invisible complexity and technical debt. Both concerns deserve weight, not dismissal — this is why the pilot and CI investment come before the wider rollout, not after it. If the pilot reveals our test suite can't catch regressions fast enough, we should slow down and fix that gap first.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
